client: I just feel so lost since my grandma passed away last month. I miss her so much, and seeing my mom struggling with her grief makes it even harder—I don't know how to comfort her when I can barely handle my own sadness. Part of me wonders if talking about it will even help, or if it'll just make us both feel worse.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a lot of grief right now, both for your grandma and for your mom, and it’s understandable to feel lost when you’re navigating so much at once. I wonder, when you think about talking about your feelings, what feels most challenging about the idea?

client:
It just feels like no one really gets it. When I try to talk about my mom or grandma, people either change the subject or give me those pitying looks. I guess the hardest part is feeling like my grief is too much for other people to handle. 

Sometimes I think maybe I should just keep it to myself because I don't want to burden anyone, but then I feel so alone with it.
therapist: It makes complete sense that you'd feel alone when the responses you're getting make your grief seem like something others can't handle—that must be incredibly isolating. I'm curious, have there been any moments when sharing your feelings actually felt helpful or connecting, even if just a little?

client: I guess there was one time when I told my cousin about missing my dad, and she actually listened without trying to fix it or change the subject. But even then, I felt guilty afterward—like I'd burdened her with my sadness. It's like every time I open up, I either scare people away or end up feeling worse for having said anything.
therapist: It sounds like that moment with your cousin was a small but meaningful connection, yet the guilt afterward made it hard to fully appreciate the comfort it brought. I wonder, what do you think might happen if you allowed yourself to believe that sharing your grief isn’t a burden, but a way to connect with those who care about you?

client:
I want to believe that sharing grief isn’t a burden, but I can’t shake the feeling that I’m just bringing everyone else down. My cousin seemed okay with it in the moment, but what if she’s just being polite? I’ve seen people pull away when things get too heavy, and I don’t want to push her away too. 

It’s like the second I start opening up, this voice in my head says, “Now they’ll see how messed up you really are.” How do I trust that people genuinely want to be there for me?
therapist: That voice telling you people will see you as "messed up" sounds so painful—it makes sense that you'd hesitate to trust connections when you're anticipating rejection. What would it feel like to consider that your cousin's willingness to listen might reflect genuine care, rather than just politeness?

client: I know my cousin probably does care, but it's hard to shake the feeling that she's just being nice out of obligation. What if I open up and she realizes how much I'm struggling? She might get overwhelmed or treat me differently afterward. That's what always happens when people see the messy parts of me.
therapist: It sounds like part of you knows your cousin cares, but there’s also this fear that if you show your vulnerability, it might change how she sees you or even push her away—that must feel really heavy to carry. I wonder, what would it be like to gently challenge the belief that opening up will always lead to people treating you differently?

client:
I get what you're saying, but every time I've opened up to people before, they either pulled away or started treating me differently. It's like once they see the messy parts of me, they can't unsee it. My cousin is one of the few people I have left—what if I ruin that too? 

The idea of challenging that belief makes me anxious because it feels like tempting fate. Like if I test it and it goes wrong, I'll have proof that my worst fear was right all along.
therapist: It makes so much sense that you'd want to protect your relationship with your cousin—when past experiences have shown people pulling away, it's natural to be cautious with your heart. I wonder if there might be a small, gentle way to test this belief without feeling like you're risking everything—what would feel like a safe first step to you?

client: I guess I could try texting her first sometimes instead of always waiting for her to reach out. But I worry that if I start initiating more, she'll feel smothered or think I'm being needy. That's what happened with my old friends when I tried to be more open with them.
therapist: It sounds like you're already imagining a middle ground—reaching out a little more while still being mindful of not overwhelming her—that shows real thoughtfulness about balancing connection and your own fears. What do you think might help you distinguish between healthy vulnerability and the patterns that didn’t work with your old friends?

client: I guess I can see the difference when I think about it—healthy vulnerability feels more like sharing small things first to test the waters, instead of dumping all my emotions at once like I used to. But it’s hard to trust that this time will be different, because what if I misread the situation again and end up pushing someone away? I keep worrying that any step forward might just lead back to the same old pattern.
therapist: You're recognizing such an important distinction—that healthy vulnerability can be gradual, like testing the waters rather than diving in all at once—and yet that fear of history repeating itself still feels so present. What would it feel like to acknowledge both: your wisdom in pacing yourself *and* the understandable worry that things might not go as hoped this time?

client: I get what you're saying about pacing myself, but it's hard to trust that gradual steps will actually protect me from getting hurt again. Part of me feels like if I open up even a little, the other person will either reject me or take advantage of my vulnerability like before. The worry feels bigger than the hope right now.
therapist: It makes complete sense that the worry outweighs the hope right now—when past hurts have taught you that vulnerability can lead to pain, trust becomes something to approach with caution. I wonder, what might help you feel just a little safer as you consider these small steps forward?

client: I don't know... every time I try to take small steps toward trusting people, my mind floods with memories of how it's backfired before. Like last week when I opened up to a coworker and they immediately started gossiping about it. It makes me feel stupid for even trying.
therapist: That must have felt so painful—to take the risk of opening up only to have it met with gossip, reinforcing those fears that vulnerability leads to hurt. I hear how exhausted you are by this cycle of hope and disappointment—what would it feel like to acknowledge both your courage in trying *and* the very real hurt when it didn’t go as you’d hoped?
